Diabetes Technology

By: Catherine Rice | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight on Carte Blanche, we take a look at the most exciting technological advancements in the management of type 1 diabetes.

Summary:
Type 1 diabetes affects millions of people around the world. It's a chronic autoimmune condition in which the body attacks and destroys the insulin producing beta cells in the pancreas. Insulin is a hormone that regulates the amount of glucose or sugar in the blood, and without it, glucose builds up in the bloodstream. If not diagnosed and treated, it's deadly. The condition typically develops in children and teenagers, but can also develop in adults. In 1921, the discovery of insulin was a game-changer for this once fatal disease. Fast forward a century, and the advances in technology have revolutionised the management of type 1 diabetes, transforming the lives of those living with the condition. The condition requires 24/7 management, and can be particularly challenging for children, who can experience isolation, depression and health complications. But, with the new developments in management, some of that burden is eliminated. We take a look at some of the most exciting advances, and how that's impacting the lives of children, from toddlers to teenagers.

Script:


VO 1 John Ray Hendricks is three - a typical toddler, curious about everything….with boundless energy. But, when the bubbly child was just a year old he became inexplicably irritable. All the time. His mother Cameron was worried.

CAMERON HENDRICKS / Mother Clip 3155 (17 March) 01:33 He showed signs of frequent urination. At that time he was on diapers and he would have about ten to twelve wet diapers just at night, wet diapers just at night. And that was very alarming for me. And he was always thirsty. And, hardly ate anything.

VO 2 A trip to the doctor confirmed a diagnosis of type 1 diabetes.

CAMERON HENDRICKS clip 3155 (17 March) 03:32 Initially, I laughed at her and said there is no way that my son who is one year old, and one month at that time can be a type 1 diabetic, with no family history whatsoever of type 1 diabetes.

VO 2a Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition - in which the body attacks the pancreas… and destroys its ability to make THE HORMONE, insulin.

Insulin is like a key…which unlocks cells to allow sugar in, that’s used as energy. Left untreated, and it very rapidly becomes deadly.

Unlike type 2 diabetes, it cannot be reversed … there is no cure. And while there is a genetic predisposition, its believed to be triggered by environmental factors, such as viruses.

MASA LINK: Clip 3092 (16 March) If type 1 diabetes is not picked up early enough by a doctor, you become at risk of a diabetic coma. Most children are admitted to hospital when they are first diagnosed, some even admitted to ICU and tragically some don’t even make it.

CAMERON HENDRICKS Clip 3156 March 17 Time code 01:10 She said we need to take him to ICU now, because it can be fatal. And I was looking at her. Tears were rolling down my face.

VO 3 Paediatric endocrinologist Dr Michelle Carihill says there is no relief from the condition, and it requires attention…. 24/7… for the rest of one’s life.

VO 3a ….and the careful balancing of blood glucose levels with the right amount of insulin.

DR Michelle Carihill / Paediatric Endocrinologist Clip 3069 March 16. Time Code: 2:10 If you give too much insulin, it takes all the sugar out of the bloodstream, you’ve got none for your brain or heart to use for energy, and if you give too little the same thing happens. In the days before insulin therapy children and young people used to die. I do want to emphasise its nobody’s fault. There’s nothing a person can do to prevent it.

MASA LINK Clip 3141 March 17 You know that awful helpless feeling you get as a parent when your child is sick, now imagine having to inject your child with needles every single day at least three times a day constantly monitoring their sugar levels with finger pricks. Now, this is what a month of daily pricking and injections looks like on your child. (with doll with needles in it next to her)

VO 4 For John Ray and his mother, the new routine took its toll.

CAMERON HENDRICKS Clip 3155 March 17 Time code: 04:44 We were trained to wake him up every two to three hours to check his sugar levels at night. MASA: Every two to three hours? 6:23 I remember him telling me mommy please don’t because it hurts. And I’m sitting there and I have to do it, I don’t have a choice.

VO 5 Cameron went on the hunt for less traumatising options for her son and discovered a range of insulin pumps and sensors.

VO 6a The insulin pump is a wearable device that delivers insulin through a small tube inserted under the skin.
Integrated with a sensor that continuously measures blood glucose levels, it mimics the job of the pancreas.
VO 6b The pump automatically adjusts insulin delivery, based on glucose readings from the sensor - an absolute game changer that eliminates the need for frequent manual adjustments with painful injections and finger pricks.

CAMERON HENDRICKS March 17 clip 3155 Time code 9:20 We had to make the decision to change, the cost was a lot and we couldn’t afford it.

VO 7 It may be the future, but for now there’s a snag - its pricey: The version of the insulin pump that looked the best for them cost at least R45,000 … that’s without the sensor that goes with it.

MASA: Clip 3069 March 16 Time code 10:20 How accessible is it for parents cos it sounds like a dream come true?
Michelle Carihill: So the problem comes with funding. It really isn’t about availability. South Africa is amazing. We have the latest technology that comes here. But it comes at a cost.

VO 8 Doctors and people living with diabetes HAVE LONG BEEN FIGHTING for ways of reducing these costs.

VO 9 But UNBELIEVABLY, Doctor Carihill, says there are no statistics on the numbers of people living with the condition in South Africa.

Doctor Michelle Carihill: Clip 3069 March 16. Time code: 03:18 Type 1 diabetes is not a notifiable disease so doctors don’t have to report it to a central authority and so there’s no national registry. Colleagues around the country are trying to remedy that.

VO 10 Living with type 1 diabetes for fifteen years, Bridget McNulty has become an advocate for diabetes awareness … tyring to get medical aids to recognise that sensor technology is revolutionary … the way of the future … and should be part of the prescribed minimum benefits - which would give all medical aid members access to it regardless of the scheme they’re on.

Bridget McNulty / SA Diabetes Advocacy Chairperson Clip 3096 March 16. Time code: 10:17 We’re appealing to the council for medical schemes to get it covered as a PMB. They have tossed out our appeal and told us that there is not enough evidence that sensor technology is superior to finger stick testing.But, there is actual hard evidence that it makes more financial sense to cover sensor technology for people with type 1 than it does to do finger sticks.

VO 12 For Bridget, sensor technology has been a revelation.

Bridget 5:54 So there’s an app on your phone and then I click scan and scan it. 06:45 And then I get a reading, and it tells me what my blood glucose is doing the whole day. 06:57 With finger sticks, best case scenario you have five to seven finger sticks a day and that’s if your medical aid is very generous, public sector have nowhere near that. That’s giving you individual points of data, they don’t tell me where you’ve been or where you’re going. What this gives me is vision.

VO 13 But ranging in price from R1000 to several thousand, they don’t come cheap.

VO 14 She believes sensor technology should be freely available, particularly for children.

Bridget Clip 3096 March 16 Time code:16:24 Medical aids have bargaining power, It’s a conversation between the advocates and the manufacturers and the medical aids, and if we could get them in bulk, then we could start talking about the public sector, and I think that’s a necessity. 19:00 When you look at the South African context, the few of us are the privileged few. And it’s wildly unfair only because its a numbers game. All type 1s in the UK have access to it. And since then, they have seen they best results they have ever seen.

VO 15 Jessica and Cameron Brown are siblings living with type 1 diabetes and both of them have the latest technology.

Jessica is 17 and was diagnosed at age 1. Cameron is 13 and was diagnosed when he was five.

VO 15a Their mother Anne Brown says when Jess was diagnosed, she nearly lost her.
Anne Brown Clip 3173 March 17 00:55 She was ketoacidotic and pretty much hours away from death.

VO 16 But, in the years since then technology has given them a sense of normality.

Anne Brown / Mother Clip 3173 March 17 Time code 05:41 They do have this gizmo attached to them but they can do so much more.
06:46 I can get an alert on my phone which is very nice when you have a teenager because you don’t have to be that hovering, helicopter parent.

VO 16a Both children are active, and spend a lot of time at the beach – the new technology is also waterproof.
Jess is a lifeguard, and Cameron is training to be one.

VO 17 The two siblings are never far apart, and at first Cameron was pleased he was like his big sister.

Cameron Brown / Clip 3179 March 17 Time code 02:35 About two weeks in, I was like I want this to go away, and my mom was like, its not going to go away, you’re stuck with it for life. And that’s when I realised this isn’t so nice.

VO 19 Jess doesn’t mind that she is attached to her insulin pump and sensor 24/7 and she doesn’t get upset when her peers don’t know what it is.

Jessica Brown (clip 3183) 03:41 A lot of my friends joke about me being a bit of a cyborg and I think that’s very funny. So it’s a bit of a personality trait.

MASA link: Clip 3212 March 17 With advancements in technology, children like Jess and Cameron can live a somewhat carefree childhood.

VO 20 People like Bridget are working every day to try and make sensor technology accessible to every child.

Bridget McNulty 17:24 We’ve already been able to see in small tests in South Africa that its cost effective, hospitalisations are so expensive …. Clip 0316 Time code 00:23 When people are decision makers, invite people living with type 1 into the room when making these decisions.

VO 21 Back in the Hendricks household, it was like Christmas when their medical aid went against the norm, and offered to pay for an insulin pump and sensor in full.

CAMERON : It changed our lives drastically, I must say.
Masa: So, no more finger pricking? So his fingers are not eina anymore.
CAMERON: Not at all. No more crying.
